content: One study combined green leafy vegetables and orange vegetables into a single category, while another grouped vegetables and leaves together. A third study specifically focused on dark green vegetables. However, for studies reporting on fruit consumption, none provided detailed information about the specific types of fruits consumed. Regarding studies on nutrient-dense plant sources (NPS), one study reported on legume consumption, and another on bean consumption. It is important to note that only two studies adjusted their analyses for confounding variables, which is a critical consideration when interpreting the results. Across the six studies included, the total sample size was 23,346 children aged 6 to 23 months at the time of enrollment. The evidence is highly uncertain regarding whether varying frequencies of consumption of dark green leafy and orange vegetables, fruits, or legumes reduce the prevalence of wasting, underweight, or stunting. One study found no association between these dietary patterns and these outcomes, contrary to expectations. Given the nutritional importance of these foods, it would be reasonable to expect that higher consumption frequencies would improve micronutrient and protein status (in the case of legumes), potentially reducing wasting, underweight, and stunting. However, while Ahmad (2018) found no association, Chang (2007) reported that less frequent fruit and vegetable consumption was associated with higher prevalence of stunting and underweight. Nevertheless, the certainty of this evidence is very low, making it difficult to determine the reliability of these findings. To date, no other studies have specifically examined the frequency of fruit and vegetable (FV) or NPS consumption and its association with nutritional status in infants. Some studies addressing similar research questions were excluded from this review due to insufficient data or ineligible exposure variables. One study demonstrated that less frequent consumption of vegetables, leaves, and fruits was associated with lower height-for-age z-scores (HAZ), while more frequent fruit consumption was positively associated with linear growth. However, the same study paradoxically found that frequent consumption of vegetables and leaves had an inverse relationship with linear growth. This finding may reflect feeding norms in the study population of rural, breastfed Senegalese infants, where mothers are educated to provide more breast milk and diverse diets to children who are ill or poorly growing. These findings were inconsistent, as the inverse relationship was not observed in children consuming vegetables at even higher frequencies. Additionally, no significant relationship was observed between vegetable feeding frequency and the likelihood of very low iron stores (ferritin <15 μg/L). The inconsistencies and low quality of the data necessitate cautious interpretation of these results. For instance, if the infants in this study consumed diets deficient in vitamin C, their ability to absorb the iron in vegetables could explain the inverse relationship observed. When a different frequency metric was used for fruit consumption (daily vs. less than daily), lower fruit consumption was associated with higher anemia prevalence. The lack of a relationship for vegetables and beans may be explained by the poor bioavailability of these foods’ iron content when not consumed with vitamin C-rich foods. The tools used to measure dietary intake, such as food frequency questionnaires (FFQs) and 24-hour recalls, have significant limitations, particularly recall bias. A single 24-hour recall, as used in this study, fails to capture irregular food consumption patterns and may underestimate nutrient intake. The use of different tools likely contributed to the variability in reported associations between fruit consumption and anemia prevalence. At follow-up points of 36 months and 7 years, boys and girls showed a downward trend in vegetable consumption from 18 months of age. Fruit consumption increased between 18 and 36 months but showed no consistent trend at 7 years. Overall, vegetable and fruit consumption at 18 months was positively associated with consumption at later ages. In the six included studies, it was not explicitly stated whether participants were food-secure. However, based on sociodemographic characteristics, at least two studies likely included food-insecure populations. Food insecurity could significantly influence the reported health and dietary outcomes, though this could not be assessed within the study populations. There was no evidence to assess the association of differing varieties of FV or amounts of NPS with primary outcomes such as stunting, wasting, or underweight. Similarly, no evidence was available to evaluate secondary outcomes like overweight/obesity, food preferences later in life, markers of inflammation, gut health, or adverse effects. The review aimed to determine the effects of varying frequencies, varieties, and amounts of FV and NPS consumed during the complementary feeding period on dietary and health outcomes. However, the evidence was limited and of very low certainty, making it impossible to establish causality. Most studies were excluded because they did not report consumption data in terms of frequency, variety, or amount. Only six studies met the eligibility criteria, and their heterogeneity in outcomes and frequency metrics precluded meta-analysis. None of the included studies provided high-certainty evidence supporting greater FV and NPS consumption for improved dietary and health outcomes, largely due to their observational nature and methodological limitations. The certainty of the evidence was rated as very low, as indicated by GRADE Evidence Profiles. This could potentially be improved with more quasi-experimental studies. Observational studies, while appropriate in some cases, require rigorous methods and consideration of confounding variables. Limitations in this review included the small sample of included studies, lack of standardized frequency metrics, and inconsistent outcome measures. The use of different tools to assess FV and NPS consumption likely contributed to mixed results and biased findings. While the search strategy was comprehensive, some studies may have been missed, potentially biasing the findings. However, publication bias is unlikely, as several included studies reported null or inconsistent findings. This is the first systematic review to examine the association between varying frequencies, varieties, and amounts of FV or NPS consumption with dietary and health outcomes. Unexpected findings included the lack of association between FV or NPS consumption and wasting, stunting, or underweight in Ahmad (2018), and the inverse relationship between vegetable consumption and linear growth in Ntab (2005). These findings may reflect feeding norms in the study populations, where caregivers are encouraged to provide more breast milk and diverse diets to ill children. Inconsistent findings were also observed for vegetable consumption and ferritin concentration, with greater vegetable consumption associated with a higher likelihood of low ferritin levels. These results highlight the need for further research with rigorous methodologies to clarify these associations.
